name: Le Fort I osteotomy

image.caption: Variations in Le Fort I osteotomy (Kurohara 2019)

lead: A Le Fort I osteotomy cuts the upper jaw free and moves it up, forward or down, correcting bite problems and long-face deformity and changing midface projection and proportion. It is also used for cleft-related deficiency and as part of sleep apnoea surgery, and it is discussed in looksmaxxing circles for reshaping the midface.

A horizontal bone cut above the tooth roots frees the maxilla, which is repositioned and fixed, usually with titanium plates and screws. The clinical literature is large but mostly observational, including a prospective evaluation of complications in 1000 patients and analyses of long-term stability by direction of movement; much of it concerns function rather than looks.

paras: It is performed by an oral and maxillofacial or craniofacial surgeon through the mouth under general anesthesia, usually planned with orthodontic care. Recovery involves weeks of restricted diet and months of bone healing, with the facial change showing as swelling settles.

Reported risks include bleeding, swelling, infection, nerve numbness, condylar resorption and, rarely, aseptic necrosis of the maxilla. In looksmaxxing forums there is sometimes disagreement about the aesthetic results. It is major jaw surgery.

angle.text: The upper jaw is cut and moved to a new position, which visibly changes midface projection and proportion along with the bite. It is discussed in looksmaxxing circles for reshaping the midface and has a large clinical literature, mostly on function.

lead: A Le Fort I osteotomy is an orthognathic (jaw) operation in which the upper jaw, or maxilla, is cut horizontally above the roots of the upper teeth, freed, moved to a new position, and fixed with titanium plates and screws, usually through incisions inside the mouth.[1][2] Because the upper jaw carries the upper teeth, the base of the nose, the upper lip and much of the cheek support, repositioning it changes how much tooth shows, how long the lower face looks, how the lip sits and how far the midface projects.[1][3] People seek it to correct bite problems and skeletal jaw discrepancies, to reduce a "gummy smile" or long-face proportion caused by vertical maxillary excess, to treat cleft-related maxillary deficiency, and, in combination with lower-jaw surgery, to enlarge the airway in obstructive sleep apnoea.[1][4][3][5]

The operation takes its name from the French surgeon René Le Fort, whose early-twentieth-century cadaver experiments described a horizontal midface fracture pattern; the surgical version was refined into its modern form by Hugo Obwegeser, often called the father of modern orthognathic surgery.[2][6][7] Maxillary movements can be up, forward, down or sideways, and the maxilla can be moved in one piece or in segments to widen or reshape the dental arch.[8][2]

The surgical literature includes a prospective evaluation of 1000 operations,[9] reports of condylar resorption and aseptic necrosis,[10][11] analyses of stability by direction of movement,[8] and randomised and registered trials comparing fixation methods and one-piece versus segmental designs.[12][13][14][15] On looksmaxxing forums the operation is discussed as one of the jaw and midface procedures within "hardmaxxing", with posters debating the aesthetic result in individual before-and-after cases.[16][17]
infobox: René Le Fort (facial-fracture classification); modern osteotomy refined by Hugo Obwegeser[2][6][7]
Often titanium plates and screws; prebent, custom and patient-specific plates under study[1][12][13]
Vertical maxillary excess, maxillary deficiency, cleft-related growth deficiency, sleep apnoea (with lower jaw)[1][2][3]
2-6 weeks initial; 2-4 more months for bone healing[1]
Bleeding, infection, numbness, nonunion, avascular necrosis[1][9][11]

paras: Vertical maxillary excess is described as showing more than a third of the upper incisors at rest and a full crown plus gum on smiling (a gummy smile), often with a long lower face and sometimes an anterior open bite.[3] A review of surgical management distinguishes total, anterior and posterior forms of the condition and describes computer-assisted preoperative planning to determine an individual surgical plan.[18] Surgery is usually combined with orthodontics; teeth are often aligned first.[3] The same sources note that jaw abnormalities can affect chewing, speech, breathing and lip closure, and that correction can improve social confidence.[1][3]

For midface projection, the maxilla can be moved forward, which is why the procedure appears in discussions of facial balance, though the effect on the cheeks, upper lip and nose base depends on the direction and size of movement and on additional steps taken at surgery.[1][2]

Jaw osteotomies are used for malocclusion from skeletal problems, airway problems including obstructive sleep apnoea, cleft-related growth deficiency, facial asymmetry and aesthetic concerns.[1] Maxillomandibular advancement for sleep apnoea was reported in 23 patients in 1989,[4] and a 2016 meta-analysis pooling 45 studies and 518 adults found the mean apnoea-hypopnoea index fell by about 80 percent, with surgical success in 85.5 percent of patients with available data and cure in 38.5 percent.[5] Wikipedia also cites a 1999 study of 50 patients for 90-100% success.[1] Segmental Le Fort I osteotomy has been compared with surgically assisted rapid maxillary expansion for transverse maxillary hypoplasia in a registered trial.[14]

The maxilla is separated from the skull base along a horizontal cut, mobilised through separation at the pterygomaxillary junction, repositioned and fixed.[2][6] Obwegeser's modern version fully mobilised the maxilla and supported bone grafting between the pterygoid plates and the tuberosities; he also described combining Le Fort I with a lower-jaw split osteotomy in a single bimaxillary operation in 1969-1970.[6] Orthognathic planning typically involves surgeons and orthodontists, uses radiographs and photographs, and can use software to predict postoperative facial shape; newer approaches include surgery-first sequences and clear aligners in place of a year of presurgical braces.[1]

A 1996 review of stability found that stability varies with direction of movement, fixation type and technique, with superior repositioning of the maxilla described as the most stable orthognathic procedure.[8] Registered trials compare one-piece with segmental osteotomy in cleft patients and prebent, custom and patient-specific plates.[12][13][15] Related terms include Le Fort II and III osteotomies, which treat other midface problems, and a disputed "Le Fort IV" label for monobloc frontofacial osteotomy.[2]

Orthognathic surgery dates to Simon Hullihen's 1849 case, with mandible and maxilla osteotomies developing in the 1940s.[1] René Le Fort described three midface fracture patterns, the first being a horizontal fracture through the maxilla also once called a Guerin fracture, from drop experiments on cadavers.[7] Obwegeser presented his orthognathic techniques to North American surgeons in 1966 and is credited with the modern Le Fort I.[6] Raffaini introduced surgery under local anaesthesia with sedation in 2002, reducing hospital time and recovery.[1]

Orthognathic surgery in general carries risks of bleeding, swelling, infection (reported up to 7% of cases) and nerve damage causing numbness, usually temporary but rarely permanent; maxillary impaction is considered a riskier movement.[1] In a prospective series of 1000 consecutive Le Fort I operations over 20 years, 6.4% of patients had complications, including nasal septum deviation (1.6%), nonunion (1.0%), transfusion-requiring bleeding (1.1%, all after bimaxillary procedures), significant infection (1.1%) and ischaemic complications (1.0%, including alveolar necrosis in 0.2%); risk was higher in craniofacial dysplasia, clefts and extensive or segmental movements.[9]

A 1990 report described 36 cases of aseptic necrosis after maxillary osteotomies,[11] and a study of 259 patients with open bite examined condylar remodelling and resorption after Le Fort I and bimaxillary osteotomies.[10] In a 2024 trial of 35 patients having maxillary, mandibular or bimaxillary surgery, Le Fort I patients showed changes in bitter-taste recognition, which the authors attributed to possible chemosensory nerve damage.[19] A registered study is examining subclinical optic nerve changes after Le Fort I.[20]

Initial healing is reported to take 2 to 6 weeks, with complete bone healing taking a further 2 to 4 months; patients often follow a liquid diet, commonly lose weight, have swelling and bruising that largely settles within weeks, and may have jaw immobilisation for 1 to 4 weeks.[1] Return to work is typically after 2 to 6 weeks with restrictions for about eight weeks.[1]

Wikipedia states that correction may improve facial aesthetics and self-esteem but that the surgery often produces a noticeable change in appearance.[1] Recent studies look at specific features. A 2026 patient-reported study of 200 patients found satisfaction with nasal appearance improved significantly after Le Fort I surgery.[21] A study in which 78 evaluators rated 26 patients with class III malocclusion after Le Fort I found that 52.5% of patients still appeared to have insufficient maxillo-zygomatic (cheek) volume, with the change in flat-volume scores not significantly different between operated and non-operated patients, and laypeople reporting flat volume less often than surgeons.[22] A 2026 study of 126 patients followed at least three years reported high satisfaction, especially with the smile, and complications in 11.1% that were linked to lower overall satisfaction.[23] In 27 patients, AI-estimated facial age did not change significantly after orthognathic surgery, while social appearance anxiety scores fell.[24] A 2026 study in female class III patients found all six rated aesthetic items higher after bimaxillary surgery.[25]

Wikipedia's article on looksmaxxing says maxillofacial surgery is frequently proposed and discussed among looksmaxxers and lists jaw surgery among the cosmetic surgeries grouped under hardmaxxing.[17] On looksmax.org, one thread compares a surgeon's pre- and post-operative images and a poster states being glad to have avoided the procedure, describing the result as unattractive; another poster says they cannot get a Le Fort III for a flat face. In another thread, a poster in Turkey whose orthodontists say a palate expander is unnecessary weighs MARPE against two- or three-piece maxillary osteotomy, hoping for a wider smile, fuller lips and more upturned eyes.[16] Such posts are individual opinions and goals, not clinical findings.

Human studies are mainly retrospective or observational: a 1000-patient prospective complication evaluation,[9] a 259-patient condylar study,[10] a 36-case necrosis report,[11] a 23-patient sleep-apnoea series[4] and a 518-patient pooled meta-analysis of maxillomandibular advancement.[5] A randomised trial compared one-year stability of splintless Le Fort I with patient-specific versus conventional osteosynthesis, and registered trials, mostly small, compare fixation and surgical techniques.[12][13][14][15] Perception studies of facial results are recent and small.[22][21][24]

lore.intro: Le Fort I is discussed on looksmax.org as one of the jaw and midface options in appearance surgery, with posters arguing about outcomes in specific before-and-after cases and about alternatives such as palate expansion.[16]

claims.claim: Le Fort I can produce an unattractive 'chimp mouth' result in some patients.
Moving the upper jaw reshapes the whole midface, lips and smile.
A palate expander can substitute for maxillary osteotomy for a wider smile.
Jaw surgery is a route to permanent facial ascension.

timeline.event: Simon Hullihen publishes one of the first jaw-surgery cases, an early precursor of orthognathic surgery.[1]
Hugo Obwegeser presents orthognathic techniques to North American surgeons in Washington, D.C.[6]
Obwegeser describes combined maxillary and mandibular (bimaxillary) surgery; the page dates the paper to 1969 or 1970.[6]
Maxillomandibular advancement for obstructive sleep apnoea reported in 23 patients.[4]
36 cases of aseptic necrosis after maxillary osteotomies reported.[11]
Review of orthognathic stability finds superior repositioning of the maxilla the most stable procedure.[8]
Study of 259 open-bite patients examines condylar resorption after Le Fort I and bimaxillary osteotomies.[10]
Raffaini introduces orthognathic surgery under local anaesthesia with sedation.[1]
Prospective evaluation of complications in 1000 Le Fort I patients.[9]
Meta-analysis of 518 adults finds large reductions in sleep-apnoea indices after maxillomandibular advancement.[5]
Patient-reported and rater-based studies of nasal, cheek and smile outcomes after Le Fort I appear.[22][21][23]
